title: Scaling Laws for Hypernetwork-Based Knowledge Injection
hook: Instead of fine-tuning to memorize facts, train a hypernetwork to generate a LoRA adapter that injects them — and it follows clean scaling laws with steeper out-of-distribution gains.
key_points: A hypernetwork is trained to map a corpus of facts to a fixed LoRA adapter that, inserted into a target model, lets it answer questions about those facts.
Reframes hypernetworks from their usual test-time adaptation to train-time knowledge injection.
Decoupling the hypernetwork's injection capacity from the target model's general ability enables the first clean scaling-law study of hypernetwork architectures.
Loss, reasoning accuracy, and OOD generalization all follow broadly predictive power laws in hypernetwork depth, width, and target size.
Beats LoRA and full fine-tuning on out-of-distribution generalization, with steeper scaling exponents.
Introduces MegaWikiQA: tens of millions of multi-hop QA pairs across 39 domains, built from Wikidata5M.
content_html: Reliably stuffing new facts into a large language model is still an open problem — fine-tuning is expensive and prone to forgetting. This paper explores a different route: train a hypernetwork (a network that outputs another network's weights) to read a corpus of facts and emit a fixed LoRA adapter that, dropped into a target model, lets it answer questions about those facts. Hypernetworks are normally used for on-the-fly test-time adaptation; here they do train-time knowledge injection.
extra_html:
The authors' key design move is to decouple the hypernetwork's injection capacity from the target model's general capability, which lets them run — for the first time — a clean scaling-law study of hypernetwork architectures. Varying hypernetwork depth, width, and target-network size, they find that loss, reasoning accuracy, and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization all follow broadly predictive power laws. Compared with LoRA fine-tuning and full fine-tuning, the hypernetwork approach shows steeper scaling exponents on every OOD evaluation, suggesting it generalizes better as it scales.

To study this at scale they built MegaWikiQA, a dataset of tens of millions of multi-hop question–answer examples spanning 39 domains, derived from Wikidata5M. The authors frame hypernetworks as a principled, scalable substrate for train-time adaptation and offer the first empirically grounded scaling laws to guide them. (Reported on arXiv; the scaling behavior and OOD advantages are the authors' claims.)

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

prereqs.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
prereqs.hook: Why retrain billions of weights when you can freeze them all and train tiny add-on matrices instead? LoRA tunes under ~1% of the parameters with near-full-fine-tune quality.
